name: Crooked Tree Wetland Fisheries (Late Archaic Maya Lowlands)
region: Crooked Tree wetlands, Belize River watershed
summary: Linear canals cut across a seasonally flooded wetland to steer annual floodwater into holding ponds, concentrating freshwater fish at harvestable density. Built by Late Archaic hunter-gatherer-fishers before maize agriculture and roughly two thousand years before Maya state formation in the region.

claims.statement: Canal-and-pond networks were engineered to convert a seasonal flood pulse into a year-round protein supply, not merely to catch fish opportunistically
Construction dates to the Late Archaic, predating maize agriculture and Maya state formation in the region
The system stayed in use for roughly two millennia across the transition from forager to farming society, outlasting the subsistence regime that built it

evidence.source: Harrison-Buck, E. et al. (2024) Late Archaic large-scale fisheries in the wetlands of the pre-Columbian Maya Lowlands, Science Advances 10(47)
AMS dates on canal fill placing initial construction at cal 2000–1900 BCE, with continued use through the Formative period
Mapped network of linear canals and associated holding ponds across the Crooked Tree Wildlife Sanctuary wetland, with freshwater faunal remains including catfish

notes: Added August 2026. Scored replication_regions=1 on purpose, even though this entry is the strongest evidence in the codex that forager-built aquaculture was invented more than once. Counting Budj Bim and Lake Tesse toward this entry's replication would apply the very criterion U-C-1 says the project has not written down. The cross-continental argument belongs in that unknown, not smuggled into a metric — see U-C-1, where this find is now the primary evidence.
